question: Hunger and food insecurity remain among the world's most pressing issues. The Global Report on Food Crises has revealed that more than 295 million people suffered from acute hunger in 2024.

In it assessment of Special Report No 1/2012: 'Effectiveness of European Union development aid for food security in sub-Saharan Africa', the Court of Auditors has concluded that the EU's action was not concentrated on at the areas with the greatest needs, its projects did not always reflect local realities and challenges and little attention was paid to results and sustainability.

The assessment flags up weaknesses both in the Commission's development cooperation efforts in sub-Saharan Africa and in work to forge stronger links between humanitarian aid and development. Considering the above: 1.

What roadmap is the Commission working on to ensure the effectiveness of development cooperation? Does the Commission’s approach also include consideration of how to strengthen the link between humanitarian aid and development?

What measures will the Commission put forward to address shortcomings in project design and monitoring, and what view does the Commission take of dialogue with local stakeholders in the implementation of these projects?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.1.2026) In line with the commitments of the Busan Forum1, the Commission has supported principles of effectiveness, including through its engagement in platforms like the Global Partnership for Effective Development Cooperation. The information on aid and development required by the Honourable Member is available on the website of the European Court of Auditors2.

This is also in line with the 19 May 2017 Council Conclusions3 on the humanitarian-development nexus. The Commission is improving project design and monitoring by reinforcing risk-based oversight and use of baselines and measurable indicators where feasible in fragile contexts. These measures aim to ensure that EU investments deliver sustained impact and contribute to the reduction of structural vulnerabilities.

Engagement with local stakeholders is built into this approach, not as a uniform model but adapted to each context. The different stakeholders are involved when conditions allow, ensuring that interventions reflect local realities and can be maintained over time.

Dialogue with civil society organisations (CSOs) is a pillar in countries’ roadmaps for civil society engagement and central to the success of partnerships with third countries. EU Delegations regularly involve civil society to collect input on priorities and concerns on programming. The Commission monitors this engagement through an annual survey on consultation and dialogue with CSOs4.
This is central to the humanitarian-development-peace approach and to the Global Gateway objective of securing durable, locally owned investments.
1 https://one.oecd.org/document/DCD/DAC/RD(2011)16/RD7/en/pdf. 2 Recommendation 2 and 3: Strengthen the implementation of the humanitarian-development- peace nexus
